source.title: Some Open Problems in Polyomino Tilings

accepted.question_text: Let a polyomino be a strongly connected union of axis-aligned unit squares on the square lattice. An isohedral tiling is a tiling of the plane by congruent copies of the polyomino such that any two copies are related by a symmetry of the tiling. If n is the number of unit-length edges on the boundary of the polyomino, is there an O(n)-time algorithm that decides whether the polyomino admits an isohedral tiling?

evidence.quote: Definitions. A polyomino is a subset of R2 formed by a strongly connected union of axis-aligned unit squares centered at locations on the square lattice Z2.
If a tiling T has the property that for all Ti, Tj∈ T , there exists a symmetry of T mapping Ti to Tj, then T is isohedral; otherwise the tiling is non-isohedral

The fastest known algorithm for testing these criteria runs in O(n log2 n) time [27], where n is the number of unit-length edges along the boundary of the polyomino. Is a faster algorithm possible? Open Problem 1 (Open Problem 2 of [27]) Is there an O(n)-time algorithm for determining whether a polyomino has an isohedral tiling?

accepted.question_text: Let a polyomino be a strongly connected union of axis-aligned unit squares on the square lattice. If a polyomino tiles the plane using only translated copies and copies rotated by 180 degrees, must it also have a tiling of that same translated-and-180-degree-rotated type that is isohedral, meaning that any two tiles are related by a symmetry of the tiling?

evidence.quote: Definitions. A polyomino is a subset of R2 formed by a strongly connected union of axis-aligned unit squares centered at locations on the square lattice Z2.
If a tiling T has the property that for all Ti, Tj∈ T , there exists a symmetry of T mapping Ti to Tj, then T is isohedral; otherwise the tiling is non-isohedral

it is unknown if this is true for tilings using other subsets of the eight possible orientations. Specifically, isohedral tilings using only translated and 180◦-rotated copies of the prototile are characterized by those polyominoes satisfying Conway’s criterion
Open Problem 2 (Open Problem 3 of [27]) Does every polyomino that has a tiling using only translated and 180◦-rotated copies also have such a tiling that is isohedral?

accepted.question_text: Let a polycube be a strongly connected union of axis-aligned unit cubes on the cubic lattice. Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether a given polycube admits an isohedral tiling of three-dimensional space?
accepted.context_brief: Algorithmic recognition of isohedral polycube tilings

evidence.quote: The three-dimensional analogs of polyominoes are polycubes: subsets of R3 formed by strongly connected unions of axis-aligned unit cubes centered at locations on the cubic lattice Z3. Just as polyominoes tile the plane, polycubes may tile three-dimensional space.
Open Problem 3 Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for determining whether a polycube has an isohedral tiling?

accepted.question_text: Let a polyomino be a strongly connected union of axis-aligned unit squares on the square lattice. Is there an algorithm that decides whether a given polyomino has any tiling of the plane at all, without restricting to isohedral tilings?

evidence.quote: Definitions. A polyomino is a subset of R2 formed by a strongly connected union of axis-aligned unit squares centered at locations on the square lattice Z2.
On the other extreme, it remains unknown whether there’s an algorithm for finding any tiling at all for a given polyomino.
Open Problem 4 Is determining whether a polyomino has a tiling decidable?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a connected polyomino that admits tilings of the plane, but every such tiling is non-periodic? In other words, is there an aperiodic polyomino?

evidence.quote: Non-isohedral tilings may be partitioned into two types: periodic tilings with (some) symmetries, and non-periodic tilings with no symmetries.
No connected shapes that have only non-periodic tilings, called aperiodic shapes, are known
Open Problem 5 Is there an aperiodic polyomino?

accepted.question_text: A tiling is k-isohedral if k is the smallest number of classes into which its tiles can be partitioned so that any two tiles in the same class are related by a symmetry of the tiling. A polyomino is k-anisohedral if it has a k-isohedral tiling but has no k'-isohedral tiling for any smaller k'. Does there exist a k-anisohedral polyomino for some k at least 7?

evidence.quote: A tiling T is k-isohedral provided that k is the smallest number of partitions in a partitioning of T such that for any two copies Ti, Tj in a common part, there is a symmetry of T mapping Ti to Tj.
A polyomino is k-anisohedral provided it has a k-isohedral tiling, but not a k′-isohedral tiling for any k′ < k.
Open Problem 6 Does there exist a k-anisohedral polyomino for some k≥ 7?

accepted.question_text: For the problem of deciding whether a polyomino has a k-isohedral tiling, where k is the parameter, is the decision problem fixed-parameter tractable?

evidence.quote: A tiling T is k-isohedral provided that k is the smallest number of partitions in a partitioning of T such that for any two copies Ti, Tj in a common part, there is a symmetry of T mapping Ti to Tj.

When attempting to determine whether a polyomino has a k-isohedral tiling, one can use a similar approach as for isohedral tilings: derive a set of sufficient boundary criteria for k-isohedral tilings, then test the polyomino against the criteria set. However, the number of such criteria grow exponentially in k
Open Problem 7 (Asked in [27]) Is determining whether a polyomino has a k-isohedral tiling in FPT?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a set consisting of exactly two polyomino prototiles that tiles the plane but has only non-periodic tilings; that is, an aperiodic set of two polyominoes?

evidence.quote: Here we consider tilings that are not monohedral: the set of prototiles contains multiple polyominoes. The introduction of multiple prototiles enables creating prototile sets that only have non-periodic tilings
Examples of aperiodic sets of just three polyominoes are known ... To the author’s knowledge, no aperiodic set of two polyominoes is known
Open Problem 8 Does there exist an an aperiodic set of two polyominoes?

accepted.question_text: Given a finite set consisting of three polyominoes, or alternatively four polyominoes, is the problem of deciding whether that set tiles the plane undecidable?

evidence.quote: Ollinger [31] proved that determining whether a set of 5 polyominoes tile the plane is undecidable
The existence of aperiodic sets of three polyominoes opens possibility that determining whether a set of just three or four polyominoes has a tiling is undecidable
Open Problem 9 (Open Problem 2 of [31]) Is determining whether a set of three (or four) polyominoes tile the plane undecidable?

accepted.question_text: Fix a polyomino P that does tile the plane. Is the decision problem 'does P tile at least one finite region?' NP-hard for every such P?
accepted.context_brief: Finite-region tiling complexity for tileable polyominoes

evidence.quote: The algorithmic problems of determining whether a given polyomino can tile a finite region have been shown to be NP-complete for the L-tromino and square (i.e., 2× 2) tetromino

these problems are closely related to the NP-hard problem of exact set cover in planar graphs ... and thus are likely NP-complete for all larger polyominoes as well. However, the author is not aware of any proof of such a result.
Open Problem 10 (Hinted at by [29]) For every polyomino P that has a plane tiling, is determining whether P can tile a finite region NP-hard?

accepted.question_text: The order of a polyomino is the minimum number of copies of that polyomino needed to tile a rectangle. Does there exist a polyomino whose order is exactly 5?

evidence.quote: Klarner [25] defined the order of a polyomino to be the minimum number of copies that can tile a rectangle.
It is also known that no polyomino has order 3 [36]. This leaves a fairly wide open spectrum of possible orders which may or may not be realized by polyominoes, the smallest of which is 5
Open Problem 11 Is there a polyomino of order 5?

accepted.question_text: A half-strip is a region obtained by intersecting a horizontal strip with a half-plane bounded by the y-axis. If a polyomino tiles some half-strip, must it also tile a rectangle?

evidence.quote: For instance, half-strip regions formed by the intersection of a horizontal strip and half-plane bounded by the y-axis.
Reid [32] asked whether tiling a half-strip implies that a rectangle can also be tiled
Open Problem 12 (Question 6 of [32]) Does every polyomino that tiles a half-strip also tile a rectangle?

accepted.question_text: A rep-tile polyomino is a polyomino that tiles a scaled copy of itself. Does every rep-tile polyomino also tile some rectangle?
accepted.context_brief: Whether all rep-tile polyominoes tile rectangles

evidence.quote: The deeply studied notion of substitution tilings [12,20] also gives rise to consideration of polyominoes that tiles scaled versions of themselves, called rep-tiles.
Many rep-tile polyominoes are known ... all of which also tile rectangles. Hochberg and Reid [24] asked whether this is true of all rep-tiles
Open Problem 13 (Asked in [24]) Does every rep-tile polyomino tile some rectangle?

accepted.question_text: An r-morphic polyomino is a polyomino that admits exactly r distinct tilings of the plane. Does there exist an r-morphic polyomino for some r greater than 10?

evidence.quote: Grünbaum and Shephard [22] considered shapes inducing a finite number of tilings r, later called r-morphic shapes [11]
later found r-morphic polyominoes for r = 4 , 5 [9], r = 6 , 7, 8, 10 [8], and r = 9 [10] ... However, no examples for larger r are known
Open Problem 14 (Asked in [22]) Does there exist an r-morphic polyomino for some r > 10?

accepted.question_text: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a polyomino and an integer r, decides whether the polyomino has exactly r distinct tilings of the plane?
accepted.context_brief: Complexity of recognizing r distinct tilings

evidence.quote: Grünbaum and Shephard [22] considered shapes inducing a finite number of tilings r, later called r-morphic shapes [11]
Following the progression in a previous section, in which the existential problem is followed by algorithmic one, how difficult is it to determine how many tilings a polyomino has?
Open Problem 15 Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for determining whether a polyomino has r distinct tilings?
